title: Bond-clean scope, inclusions and exclusions
audience: Bond and end-of-lease cleaners who agree scope with the customer before the clean.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: Consumer Affairs Victoria, Condition reports (renting) (last updated 14 October 2026); Consumer Affairs Victoria, Releasing or claiming the bond (landlords and owners) (last updated 14 October 2026); Residential Tenancies Authority (RTA), Queensland, Exit condition report (no date shown); NSW Government, Moving out of a rental home (last updated 19 May 2025); NSW Government, Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy (no date in body; metadata published 15 September 2023, modified 14 September 2026); Consumer Protection, Western Australia, Moving out of a rental (last updated 18 September 2026); South Australian Government, Bond refunds (last updated 19 October 2021); Consumer, Building and Occupational Services (CBOS), Tasmania, Moving out advice for tenants (last updated 8 August 2022); ACT Government, Ending a tenancy (no date shown); NT Consumer Affairs, A guide to renting in the Northern Territory (cover dated February 2026, version 4.3; no date in body).
learningOutcomes: Read the accepted work order and separate cleaning from restoration and specialist work.
Document pre-existing damage, inaccessible areas and fragile materials before work.
Decline to promise bond return or extra work that has not been priced and approved.

instruction.heading: The work order decides the scope
instruction.body: A bond or end-of-lease clean is defined by the customer's accepted work order and the applicable tenancy arrangements. It is not a promise that the bond will be returned. Identify the rooms, fixtures, surfaces, access conditions and the specific deliverables before you start. Where the work order and the customer's expectation differ, record the difference and get approval before you proceed.

instruction.heading: Cleaning is not restoration
instruction.body: Normal soil removal differs from repairing damage, removing permanent stains, remediating mould, controlling pests or working at height. Record these as exclusions, and refer them to a qualified service where they are needed. A cracked tile is recorded as damage, not as a cleaning failure.

instruction.heading: Checkpoints and changes
instruction.body: Before work, document pre-existing damage, inaccessible areas, fragile materials, power and water constraints, and unusually heavy soil. In Victoria, the start-of-tenancy condition report, together with any photos taken then, is the comparison point at the end of the tenancy, and a rental provider cannot claim for ordinary wear (Consumer Affairs Victoria, releasing or claiming the bond, last updated 14 Oct 2026). When a client asks for an extra oven, balcony or carpet extraction, check training, tools, hazards and pricing authority before agreeing. Do not promise extra work on behalf of the business without approval. Conditions vary by state, territory and country. The local law and the manufacturer's instructions govern, and this lesson does not substitute for them.

procedure: Read the accepted work order and the tenancy arrangements that apply.
Identify rooms, fixtures, surfaces, access and the specific deliverables.
Record pre-existing damage, inaccessible areas and fragile materials before work.
Record exclusions that need a separate qualified service.
Check training, tools, hazards and pricing before agreeing any extra task.

workedExamples.situation: The client assumes carpet steam cleaning is included, but the work order lists vacuuming only.
workedExamples.reasoning: Point to the work order and document the difference. Request approval and pricing for the carpet cleaning rather than making a promise that the work order does not support.

equipmentAndPpe: Signed work order and the pre-work checklist.
Camera for pre-existing defects, used with permission.

commonErrors.prevention: Victoria releases a bond only when the named parties agree or a tribunal orders it, and the cleaner is not one of those parties (Consumer Affairs Victoria, releasing or claiming the bond, last updated 14 Oct 2026).
Price and approve extra work before doing it.

commonErrors.error: Recording a cracked tile as a cleaning failure.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Mould remediation, pest control and high-access work are outside a routine bond clean and are referred to qualified services. This is practice guidance, not a legal rule.

Victoria: the rental provider has 10 days from the end of the agreement to finish the exit condition report. Renters must leave the property reasonably clean, allowing for ordinary wear (Consumer Affairs Victoria, condition reports, last updated 14 Oct 2026). For agreements signed from 29 March 2021, a rental provider may demand professional cleaning only where the property must be restored to its starting state, or where it is already in a condition that calls for it (same page).

Victoria bond release: a bond is paid out only when every party named on it agrees, or when a VCAT order directs it. A rental provider has 14 days from the end of the agreement to start a claim, and must tell the renter three business days ahead of lodging it (Consumer Affairs Victoria, releasing or claiming the bond, last updated 14 Oct 2026).

Queensland: the tenant and the property manager should complete the exit condition report together. The tenant must thoroughly clean the property, and the manager must deliver the finished version to the renter's new address inside three business days (RTA Queensland, exit condition report, no date shown). Supporting evidence for a bond claim must be provided no later than 14 days after the claim is raised (same page). The page does not say whether professional cleaning or cleaning receipts are required.

New South Wales: the renter should hand the premises back close to its move-in state and repair damage beyond ordinary wear (NSW Government, moving out of a rental home, last updated 19 May 2025). The bond page says the landlord or agent has 14 days to accept a claim made online, or 14 days to dispute a paper claim, and describes the cleaning standard as matching the original condition (NSW Government, getting your bond back, metadata modified 14 Sep 2026). Neither page sets a professional-cleaning requirement.

Western Australia: the tenant is expected to hand the home back close to its move-in state and pay for damage beyond ordinary wear. The page gives no day count for the final inspection or the bond release, and does not require professional cleaning or receipts (Consumer Protection WA, moving out of a rental, last updated 18 Sep 2026).

South Australia: the official bond refunds page (last updated 19 Oct 2021) sets no cleaning standard and gives no day count for the landlord or the refund. It recommends that tenants record the property's state with photos on departure, but does not make that mandatory (sa.gov.au, bond refunds, last updated 19 Oct 2021).

Tasmania: the official moving-out page (last updated 8 Aug 2022) says the property should go back as it was when the tenancy began, and that carpets need a professional cleaner, with the receipt kept (CBOS Tasmania, moving-out advice, last updated 8 Aug 2022). It gives no day count for the exit report or the bond refund.

Australian Capital Territory: the official ending-a-tenancy page says the property should match its move-in condition for cleanliness and repair, with some wear excepted. It gives no day count and does not say whether professional cleaning or receipts are needed (ACT Government, ending a tenancy, no date shown).

Northern Territory: the NT Consumer Affairs guide (cover dated February 2026, version 4.3) expects tenants to return the premises in a reasonably clean condition, allowing for normal wear (NT Consumer Affairs, guide to renting, February 2026). The guide also says a lease term forcing carpet steam-cleaning is not lawful under the Act, and that the landlord must pay the bond back seven business days after the tenant moves out (same guide).

qualityStandard: Work order read and scope confirmed before the simulated clean.
Pre-existing damage and exclusions recorded before work.
Extra work held until priced and approved, in the case study.
documentationEvidence: Pre-work checklist with pre-existing damage and exclusions.
summary: The accepted work order sets the scope.
Cleaning is not restoration; record exclusions.
Do not promise bond return or unapproved extra work.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client expects carpet steam cleaning, but the work order lists vacuuming only. What is correct?
options: Steam clean it anyway, since the client expects it
Vacuum and say nothing about the difference to the client
Document the difference and request approval and pricing

knowledgeChecks.question: Is a cracked tile a cleaning failure?
options: No, it is recorded as pre-existing damage
Yes, the cracked tile is a cleaning failure
Yes, if it is dirty when the clean finishes

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a cleaner promise bond return?
options: Yes, always, once the clean is signed off
No, the cleaner does not decide the bond
Yes, for a small fee paid to the agent
